video_title: How Long Could You Survive Ebola?

segments.segment_title: How Long Could You Survive Ebola
segments.text:
An exciting expedition through the forests of West Africa is about to take a deadly turn. A startled bat comes out of nowhere
and sinks its teeth into your hand, injecting the Ebola virus into your bloodstream. This hemorrhagic fever virus is notorious for intense inflammation and tissue damage throughout the body. Ebola disrupts the body's clotting mechanism, potentially resulting in internal
and external bleeding. No wonder it has an average fatality rate of 50%. Brace yourself, because things are going to get ugly. Like, bleeding from your eyes ugly. When will the first symptoms appear?

segments.segment_title: Symptoms include bleeding from eyes, rapid progression, and potential death.
segments.text:
What can you do to fight it? And how long do you have until the virus kills you? The answers to these questions and more as we put you in the shoes of an Ebola victim. But for now, let's go to the moment of exposure. The Ebola virus enters your body through broken skin or mucous membranes in your mouth, nose or eyes. Once it's inside you, the virus wastes
no time in launching its assault. It infiltrates your immune cells,
particularly your microphages. The guardians tasked with protecting your body
against invaders. The sneaky virus hijacks the cells, forcing them to produce countless copies of itself. This marks the beginning of a relentless attack
against your body's defenses. The worst part? You won't feel a thing. You are a ticking viral time bomb. But the invasion won't stay silent for long. You might feel
something is wrong before the end of a week. As the incubation period progresses,
the virus gradually spreads throughout your body,
infiltrating your tissues and organs. Common early symptoms of Ebola include fever,
usually accompanied by headache, muscle pain and fatigue. Initially, these symptoms might be mild
and nonspecific, like a common cold. At this point, you'll be taking some over-the-counter
medications to control your fever and pain. But by day seven,
brace yourself for a hellish experience. This virus is ready to show its true colors. You'll know something is definitely wrong
when you start feeling sharp abdominal pains. Your gastrointestinal tract is under siege, causing
constant diarrhea and vomiting,
which leads to severe dehydration. I know it sounds bad already,
but we're just getting started. Ebola causes significant damage
to the liver, compromising its function and leading to a condition known as viral hepatitis. This will likely lead to jaundice. That's the yellowing of the skin and eyes.

segments.segment_title: Buildup of bilirubin in bloodstream indicates need for medical attention.
segments.text:
Due to the buildup of bilirubin in your bloodstream. By now, you're probably aware
that this is not a typical flu and you should be getting medical attention ASAP. Also, at this point,
your body's fluids are spreading the virus, so you should isolate and have a private bathroom
until you get some tests done. If you're certain that you have Ebola,
it's important now to retrace your steps over the last few days
and determine the source of the virus. Identifying the cause of an outbreak early on can save your life and those around you. This virus can't fool your immune system forever. For the next 1 to 2 weeks. Your body will mount its counter attack. Immune cells called B lymphocytes
kick into gear and make antibodies which latch on to the virus
and stop it from infecting more of your cells. Then another branch of the immune system activates
producing T cells that go around hunting down
and destroying the infected cells. Sounds like a good thing, right? Well, with Ebola, it's never that simple. In some cases, the immune response to the infection
gets out of control, leading to a phenomenon known as a cytokine storm. This happens
when you produce too many chemicals called cytokines, causing inflammation and damage to the body. Cytokines are small proteins that help control
the activity and growth of your immune cells and blood cells. If your body produces too many of them,
the results can be deadly. You can expect high fever, trouble breathing, vomiting and diarrhea. If your sickness gets worse, doctors may use drugs to reduce inflammation and lower your fever, and you'll need to get IV fluids
to prevent extreme dehydration. But the complications get a little more serious
when you reach the 14 day mark. The infection may start to spread rapidly through your bloodstream, causing septic shock. This dangerous drop in blood
pressure can lead to organ failure and in some situations, death. Ebola can mess with your kidneys, too,
making it harder for them to clean your blood
and to keep the right balance of salts and minerals. One particularly frightening complication
is disseminated intravascular coagulation or DIC, which is a fancy way of saying that the body's blood clotting system has gone haywire. This is scary. DIC may cause bleeding from the gums and eyes to the gastrointestinal tract and even the brain and it's usually the most life
threatening aspect of the disease. This means all hands on deck for the medical team. They'll continue the fluids to keep you hydrated, assisted ventilation to keep enough oxygen in your body and even dialysis to help clear waste from your blood.

segments.segment_title: Vasopressor drugs and isolation are crucial for treatment.
segments.text:
They might also have to use vasopressor drugs
to help raise blood pressure and give you medications to help your blood clot. At this stage, you'll have to be isolated
and the doctors treating you will have to wear masks
and biohazard suits to avoid contagion. The third week marks a crucial point where you can begin to recover or get closer to dying. Survival rates during this phase
depend on different things, like how old the person is, how healthy they were before getting sick and
whether or not they have access to good medical care. For some, the body might be able to fight off the virus
and start healing. But for others, the illness might get more severe,
making it harder to recover. There is no specific treatment for Ebola. What doctors do is treat the symptoms
and hope that the body is able to fight off the virus.

segments.segment_title: Ervebo vaccine has been effective in combating Ebola spread.
segments.text:
According to the CDC, there's no universal
Ebola vaccine yet. However, the first FDA approved
Ebola vaccine called Ervebo has worked wonders
in stopping the spread of the Zaire strain. It's mainly given to high risk individuals like family members of patients or health care workers. After 21 days, severe complications of Ebola
like hemorrhagic fever and systemic organ failure can lead to shock and ultimately kill you. When handling deceased individuals infected with Ebola proper personal protective equipment is essential. The virus remains contagious. Even after death, thanks to its resilience
to moderate temperature shifts. Now, if you were lucky enough to detect the illness early and get quick medical attention, you'd likely be part of the 50% that survives Ebola. But don't go celebrating just yet. You might continue to experience body aches
and weakness for weeks or even months after recovering from Ebola. And for the men watching, don't think you're safe to... Well, get it on at this point. You're advised to wait three months
before having sexual relations. Since the virus will still be present
in other body fluids. for women,
it's recommended to refrain from breastfeeding until after you've consulted with a health care
professional. The good news is that you might have ten years
of immunity against the virus now, but scientists have yet to establish
if this applies to all subtypes of Ebola. So don't press your luck. Ebola’s 50% fatality rate is scary, but that's nothing compared to rabies. Once you develop the symptoms, rabies has a 99.9% chance of killing you. Learn how to stop it in time here, on How to Survive.
